_**User**_

based on this setup and run keeping in mind that this app needs to published on aws - "Create an empty database, e.g.:

createdb ekatma_dham
# or in psql:  CREATE DATABASE ekatma_dham;

2. Get the code
git clone <your-repo-url> ekatma-dham
cd ekatma-dham
npm install

(Don't run npm install inside the Replit shell — only on your local machine.)

3. Collect the secret values from Replit
In this Repl, open Tools → Secrets (lock icon in the left panel) and copy these values to a safe place. You'll paste them into your local .env in the next step.

Key	Required?	What it's for
DATABASE_URL	Yes (use your local one, not Replit's)	Postgres connection string
SESSION_SECRET	Yes	Signs Express session cookies; any long random string works
OPENAI_API_KEY	Strongly recommended	AI word-by-word meanings + translation tools
STRAPI_URL	Optional	Enables the Strapi CMS as a content source
STRAPI_API_TOKEN	Optional	Auth for the Strapi CMS
GEMINI_API_KEY	Optional	Used only by a couple of translation scripts
REPL_ID	Optional (login won't work locally without it)	Replit OIDC client id
ISSUER_URL	Optional	Defaults to https://replit.com/oidc if unset
PORT	Optional	Defaults to 5000 (server/index.ts:86)
Replit's own DATABASE_URL points at Replit's managed Postgres — don't reuse it locally; use your own local/cloud Postgres URL instead.

4. Create a local .env
The codebase doesn't use dotenv, so you have two clean options. Pick one — option B is what I'd recommend.

Option A — export in your shell each time
export DATABASE_URL="postgres://postgres:postgres@localhost:5432/ekatma_dham"
export SESSION_SECRET="change-me-to-a-long-random-string"
export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."
# optional:
export STRAPI_URL="https://...your-strapi..."
export STRAPI_API_TOKEN="..."
npm run dev

Option B — use a .env file (recommended)
Create .env at the project root:
DATABASE_URL=postgres://postgres:postgres@localhost:5432/ekatma_dham
SESSION_SECRET=change-me-to-a-long-random-string
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
# optional:
STRAPI_URL=https://...your-strapi...
STRAPI_API_TOKEN=...
# GEMINI_API_KEY=...
# REPL_ID=...
# ISSUER_URL=...
# PORT=5000

Make sure .env is git-ignored (it already is via the existing .gitignore patterns — verify it doesn't get committed).

Run with dotenv-cli so you don't have to touch any code:

npx dotenv-cli -e .env -- npm run dev

Either option works — the app just reads process.env.*.

If you'd prefer the app to load .env automatically without dotenv-cli, you'd add import "dotenv/config"; at the top of server/index.ts. That's a code change though — say the word and I can queue a task for it.

5. Push the database schema
With DATABASE_URL pointing at your empty Postgres database:

npm run db:push

This runs drizzle-kit push and creates all the tables defined in shared/schema.ts (no migration files involved).

6. Start the app
npm run dev
# or, with option B:
npx dotenv-cli -e .env -- npm run dev

Then open: http://localhost:5000

What happens on first boot:

Express + Vite boot on port 5000.
runSeedOperations() (server/index.ts:101-124) runs through ~14 seeders: Isha Upanishad, Bhagavad Gita, Katha Upanishad, word meanings, translations, etc. Expect the first start to take a couple of minutes and print a lot of [Katha] Seeding…-style logs.
If STRAPI_URL + STRAPI_API_TOKEN are set, prewarmAllBookCaches() (server/index.ts:126-154) pre-fetches every grantha into an in-memory cache.
Subsequent starts are fast — every seeder checks for existing rows and exits early.
If a seeder errors out, the server still keeps running (each seeder is wrapped in .catch(console.error)), so don't panic over a single red line.

7. Production build (optional)
npm run build   # bundles client (Vite) + server (esbuild) into dist/
NODE_ENV=production node dist/index.cjs
# or simply:
npm start

In production mode, Vite middleware is replaced by serveStatic (server/index.ts:79-84), which serves dist/public.

8. Things to know that are specific to this project
Login (Replit OIDC) won't work locally. server/replit_integrations/auth/replitAuth.ts reads process.env.REPL_ID (line 15) and process.env.ISSUER_URL (line 14, with a default of https://replit.com/oidc). Even if you copy REPL_ID over, the OIDC redirect is registered for Replit's domain, not localhost. Practical impact: the app loads fine, you just can't sign in, and per-user features (notes, reading progress) will be hidden. You'd need to swap in a different auth provider for local login — out of scope here.
Strapi is optional. Without STRAPI_URL / STRAPI_API_TOKEN, HybridStorage (server/storage.ts) silently falls back to local Postgres. You'll only see the books seeded by server/seed.ts, seed-gita.ts, and seed-katha-upanishad.ts. The "two Kathopanishads" duplicate you saw earlier only appears when Strapi is reachable.
Replit-only Vite plugins. vite.config.ts loads @replit/vite-plugin-cartographer and @replit/vite-plugin-dev-banner only when process.env.REPL_ID is defined — so locally they're skipped automatically. @replit/vite-plugin-runtime-error-modal always loads but is harmless.
Port is 5000. Override with PORT=3000 npm run dev if 5000 is taken.
package.json is locked. The skill rules (and good sense) say not to edit it. If you need a new dependency, install it with npm install <pkg> rather than hand-editing.
9. Troubleshooting cheat sheet
Symptom	Likely cause / fix
DATABASE_URL, ensure the database is provisioned	DATABASE_URL not set in your shell / .env.
password authentication failed	Wrong user/pass in DATABASE_URL.
relation "books" does not exist	You skipped step 5 — run npm run db:push.
EADDRINUSE :::5000	Port already in use. Run PORT=5050 npm run dev.
App loads but books list is empty	Seeders haven't finished yet, or they errored — check the terminal logs.
AI word-meaning calls 500	OPENAI_API_KEY not set or invalid.
"Sign in" button does nothing	Expected locally — Replit OIDC isn't usable outside Replit.
Only one Kathopanishad shows	Expected if STRAPI_URL isn't set — the duplicate is a Strapi-vs-DB merge issue.
That's the whole flow. Want me to queue a task to (a) add a proper .env.example to the repo and (b) wire dotenv into server/index.ts so npm run dev "just works" locally without dotenv-cli? Both would be small, safe changes — just say the word."

Here is how your local/Replit flow lines up with **AWS**, what was wrong in the repo, and what was changed.

## AWS mapping for your numbered flow

| Step | Local / Replit | On AWS |
|------|----------------|--------|
| **DB** | `createdb` locally | **Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL** (new empty DB, security group allows your app only). Use the RDS endpoint in `DATABASE_URL`; append `?sslmode=require` if your driver expects TLS. |
| **Secrets** | Replit Secrets → `.env` | **Secrets Manager** or **SSM Parameter Store** (encrypted). Inject at runtime as env vars on **ECS**, **App Runner**, **Elastic Beanstalk**, or **Lambda** (if you adapt the server). Never bake secrets into the image. |
| **`.env`** | File + `dotenv-cli` | No `.env` file in the image; set the same variable **names** in the task/service configuration. |
| **`db:push`** | `npm run db:push` | Run once per environment (e.g. CI job or one-off ECS task) against that env’s `DATABASE_URL`. **Note:** your `npm run build` currently runs `drizzle-kit push` inside `script/build.ts`, so a **production build already tries to push schema** and needs `DATABASE_URL` at build time. If you prefer “build in CI without DB access,” split schema push out of `build.ts` later. |
| **Run** | `npm run dev` | `NODE_ENV=production`: `npm run build` then `npm start` (or run the built `dist/index.cjs` with the same env). **HTTPS** in front (ALB / CloudFront): you already use `app.set("trust proxy", 1)`, which is correct behind a proxy. |
| **Port** | `PORT` default 5000 | Many AWS runtimes set **`PORT`** (often **8080**). Your server reads `process.env.PORT`, so align the container/target port with that. |
| **Auth** | Replit OIDC | Replit redirects are tied to Replit; on AWS, **`REPL_ID` is usually omitted**. The app now **starts without** Replit OIDC and logs a warning; users can use **email/password** (`/api/auth/register`, `/api/auth/login`) instead, unless you add Cognito or similar later. |

## Repo fixes (so AWS/local match your doc)

1. **`.env` was not ignored** — root `.gitignore` only had `node_modules` / `dist`. It now ignores `.env` / `.env.*` and keeps **`.env.example`** tracked.

2. **`.env` loading** — Added the `dotenv` dependency and `import "dotenv/config"` at the top of `server/index.ts`, plus the same in `drizzle.config.ts`, so `npm run dev` and `npm run db:push` pick up a root `.env` without `dotenv-cli`.

3. **`setupAuth` required `REPL_ID`** — Without it, OIDC discovery could break startup on AWS. Replit routes are now registered **only when `REPL_ID` is set**; otherwise session + Passport still run for email auth.

4. **Session cookies** — `secure` is now **`true` only when `NODE_ENV === "production"`**, so local HTTP dev can still set cookies; on AWS use **HTTPS** in production (as you should anyway).

5. **`.env.example`** — Template with short **RDS / PORT / auth** notes for operators.

## Optional AWS sharp edges (no code change)

- **`httpServer.listen({ reusePort: true })`**: rare, but if the process fails to bind in a container, try dropping `reusePort` in a follow-up.
- **First boot**: same as local — seeders can take minutes; size the task health check **start period** accordingly (ECS / Beanstalk).
- **`OPENAI_API_KEY` / Strapi**: same semantics as your cheat sheet; outbound HTTPS to OpenAI/Strapi must be allowed from the VPC/subnet.

If you want next steps in-repo, the highest-value follow-up is **decoupling `drizzle-kit push` from `npm run build`** so CI builds do not need DB credentials or mutate production during every deploy. I can do that in a separate change if you want.

_**Agent (default)**_

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
The user wants to know how to configure a database that can be accessed by customers when the application is live.</details></think>

_**Agent (default)**_

Customers never talk to your database directly. They hit your **app** (HTTPS). The app server uses **`DATABASE_URL`** to talk to Postgres on a private network. “Accessible to customers” really means **accessible to your deployed app**, reliably and safely.

## What you need

1. **Managed Postgres in the cloud** (same region as the app), not `localhost`.
2. **A connection string** your app uses in production: host, port, database name, user, password, and usually **`?sslmode=require`** for TLS.
3. **Network rules** so only your app can connect (not the whole internet).

## On AWS (fits your earlier plan)

**Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL**

- Create an RDS instance (engine PostgreSQL, pick a size, enable storage/automated backups as you like).
- Put it in a **VPC**. Prefer:
  - **Private subnets** for RDS (no public IP).
  - **Security group on RDS**: inbound **5432** (or your port) **only** from the security group attached to your app (ECS tasks, Elastic Beanstalk instances, App Runner connector, etc.) — not `0.0.0.0/0`.
- Create a **database user** and password; store them in **Secrets Manager** (or SSM) and inject as **`DATABASE_URL`** on the service that runs `node dist/index.cjs` (or your container).

Your customers only see the app URL; RDS stays internal.

## If the app is not on AWS yet

Same idea anywhere:

- **Neon**, **Supabase**, **Railway**, **Render Postgres**, **Google Cloud SQL**, **Azure Database for PostgreSQL**, etc.
- You get a **hosted connection string**; you put that in production env vars; you lock down **IP allowlists** or **VPC peering** depending on the product.

## Things that often trip people up

- **Using a local DB** for production — customers’ browsers never reach it; only your laptop would. Production needs a URL that resolves from **where the server runs** (ECS/Beanstalk/VM), not from your home machine.
- **Opening RDS to 0.0.0.0/0** — convenient for debugging, bad for security. Prefer app SG → RDS SG only.
- **Migrations / `db:push`** — run against that same production DB from CI or a one-off job with the production `DATABASE_URL`, not from random laptops with a copy-pasted URL in chat.

If you say whether you’re targeting **RDS + ECS**, **Elastic Beanstalk**, or **App Runner**, the exact “where to paste `DATABASE_URL`” step names differ slightly but the database side is the same: hosted Postgres + SG rules + secret env var.

`psql` on your machine is **PostgreSQL 15 (Homebrew)**. A local URL is not one fixed string for everyone: it depends on **username**, **password**, and **database name** you chose when you set Postgres up.

## URL shape

Use either prefix (both work with `pg` / Drizzle):

```text
postgresql://USER:PASSWORD@HOST:PORT/DATABASE_NAME
```

Example if user is `postgres`, password is `postgres`, DB is `ekatma_dham`, default port:

```text
postgresql://postgres:postgres@localhost:5432/ekatma_dham
```

## Typical Homebrew on macOS

- **Host:** `localhost` or `127.0.0.1`
- **Port:** `5432` unless you changed it
- **User:** often your **macOS login name** for peer/socket login, or `postgres` if you created that role
- **Password:** whatever you set (Homebrew sometimes uses **trust** on the socket so a password is only required over TCP)

## Create DB (if needed)

```bash
createdb ekatma_dham
```

Or:

```bash
psql -d postgres -c 'CREATE DATABASE ekatma_dham;'
```

Use `-d postgres` (or `template1`) so you are not connecting to a DB that does not exist yet.

## See what actually works on your machine

In a normal terminal (so it can prompt if needed):

```bash
psql -h localhost -p 5432 -U YOUR_USER -d ekatma_dham -c '\conninfo'
```

When that connects, your `DATABASE_URL` is:

```text
postgresql://YOUR_USER:YOUR_PASSWORD@localhost:5432/ekatma_dham
```

If you use **no password** over localhost, some setups still want a URL like:

```text
postgresql://YOUR_USER@localhost:5432/ekatma_dham
```

If your driver complains, try adding an empty password section only if your client requires it (many accept the form above).

Put the final line in your project root `.env` as:

```env
DATABASE_URL=postgresql://...
```

If you tell me your **DB name** and whether you log in as **`postgres`** or your **mac username**, the only missing piece is the password you set (you should not paste the real password here); the rest of the URL is fixed from that.

## 1. Pick the right Postgres (you have 15 and 18)

Your `psql` is from **PostgreSQL 15**:

`/opt/homebrew/opt/postgresql@15/bin/psql`

Use the **data directory for the server you actually run** (usually the same major version). Common Homebrew data path:

`/opt/homebrew/var/postgresql@15`

If your service is `@18`, use `postgresql@18` there instead. Check:

```bash
brew services list
```

## 2. Stop the server

```bash
brew services stop postgresql@15
```

(Use `postgresql@18` if that is what is running.)

## 3. Edit `pg_hba.conf`

Open the file inside the data directory, e.g.:

`/opt/homebrew/var/postgresql@15/pg_hba.conf`

Find lines for **`local`** and **`host`** … **`127.0.0.1/32`** (and **`::1/128`** if present). The last field is often **`scram-sha-256`** or **`md5`**.

For **only** those local / loopback lines, change that last field to **`trust`** (temporarily).  
Save the file.

## 4. Start Postgres again

```bash
brew services start postgresql@15
```

## 5. Connect without a password and set a new password

Use the **same username** your URL uses (from the prompt, likely **`chitrajain`**):

```bash
psql -h localhost -U chitrajain -d postgres
```

Then in `psql`:

```sql
ALTER ROLE chitrajain WITH PASSWORD 'choose-a-new-strong-password';
```

If you use role **`postgres`** instead:

```bash
psql -h localhost -U postgres -d postgres
```

```sql
ALTER ROLE postgres WITH PASSWORD 'choose-a-new-strong-password';
```

Type `\q` to quit.

## 6. Put security back

Edit **`pg_hba.conf`** again and change those lines back from **`trust`** to **`scram-sha-256`** (or whatever they were before).

Restart:

```bash
brew services restart postgresql@15
```

## 7. Update your app

Set **`DATABASE_URL`** (and any tools using the DB) to use the **new** password.


(If that fails, check `brew info postgresql@15` for the data path Homebrew expects.) Use the `data_directory` path it prints to find the real **`pg_hba.conf`**.

### If you want to set a new password for `postgres`

At the `postgres=#` prompt run:

```sql
ALTER ROLE postgres WITH PASSWORD 'your-new-strong-password';
```

Then `\q` to exit.

Put that password in your app `.env`:

```env
DATABASE_URL=postgresql://postgres:your-new-strong-password@localhost:5432/your_database_name
```

(Create the DB first if needed: `CREATE DATABASE your_database_name;`)

### About the version message

- **Client:** PostgreSQL 15 (`psql` from Homebrew `@15`)
- **Server:** PostgreSQL 17

So whatever is listening on **port 5432** is **Postgres 17**, not the `@15` service we discussed earlier. That is fine for normal use; for fewer surprises you can use the 17 client when talking to a 17 server, for example:

```bash
/opt/homebrew/opt/postgresql@17/bin/psql -U postgres
```

(if that path exists after `brew install postgresql@17`).

### Practical takeaway

Use **`DATABASE_URL` against this server (17)** for Sacred-Script-Hub if that is the instance on `localhost:5432`. If you intended to use **only** `postgresql@15`, something else (17) is bound to 5432; run `brew services list` and check anything named `postgresql` or use `lsof -i :5432` on your machine to see which binary owns the port.

Here is what happened:

### Code fix (already in the repo)

Startup was failing with **`Invalid URL`** because **`ISSUER_URL=`** in `.env` is an **empty string**. `??` does not replace `""`, so the code tried `new URL("")`. That is fixed so a blank **`ISSUER_URL`** falls back to Replit’s default issuer, and blank **`REPL_ID`** still disables OIDC.

### Run result

1. **Port 5000** — Already in use (`EADDRINUSE`). The app was started successfully on **`PORT=5050`** instead.

2. **`getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND base`** — Postgres is trying to connect to host **`base`**. That comes from a **bad `DATABASE_URL`**, not from the app logic. Typical causes:
   - A placeholder host like **`@base:`** left in the URL
   - A **typo** or truncated line
   - A password with **`@`** (or other special characters) **not URL-encoded**, so the parser treats part of the password as the host (sometimes you can end up with a bogus host like `base`)

   Your URL should look like this (adjust user, password, db name):

   ```env
   DATABASE_URL=postgresql://postgres:YOUR_PASSWORD@localhost:5432/sacred_script_hub
   ```

   If the password contains `@`, `#`, `/`, etc., encode it (e.g. `@` → `%40`). You can build it with:

   ```bash
   node -e "console.log('postgresql://postgres:' + encodeURIComponent('YOUR_RAW_PASSWORD') + '@localhost:5432/sacred_script_hub')"
   ```

### What you should do

1. **Fix `DATABASE_URL`** in `.env` as above (host **`localhost`**, correct DB name, encoded password if needed).
2. **Free port 5000** (optional): quit the other dev server, or keep using **`PORT=5050`**.
3. **Restart**:

   ```bash
   npm run dev
   ```

   Or, if 5000 is still taken:

   ```bash
   PORT=5050 npm run dev
   ```

4. Open **`http://localhost:5050`** (or **`http://localhost:5000`** if you use the default port).

I’m not opening your `.env` here (secrets). After you correct **`DATABASE_URL`**, run **`npm run db:push`** once if tables are not created yet.

_**Agent (default)**_

Here is what was going wrong and what we changed.

### Root cause: `ENOTFOUND base`

`pg` was resolving **`base`** as the database **hostname**. That only happens when **`DATABASE_URL` is wrong** (for example `...@base:5432/...`, a bad copy/paste, or a **`#` in the password** so dotenv treats the rest of the line as a comment and the URL is truncated in a way that still parses but points at a bogus host).

**Fix in your `.env`:** use a real host, usually:

`postgresql://postgres:YOUR_PASSWORD@localhost:5432/sacred_script_hub`

If the password contains **`#`**, wrap the **whole** value in double quotes. If it contains **`@`**, use **`%40`** instead of `@` in the password part.

---

### Code changes (repo)

1. **`server/database-url.ts`**  
   - Trims the URL, strips wrapping quotes, parses with **`pg-connection-string`**, and **throws once** with a clear message (including the bogus **`base`** case).  
   - Syncs **`process.env.DATABASE_URL`** so session/Postgres use the same cleaned string.

2. **`server/db.ts`** and **`drizzle.config.ts`**  
   - Use **`resolveDatabaseUrl()`** so bad URLs fail **immediately** instead of spamming `getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND base`.

3. **`server/strapi.ts`**  
   - **`STRAPI_URL`** / **`STRAPI_API_TOKEN`** are **trimmed** (trailing `/` removed on the URL).  
   - If the Strapi probe fails, it logs **once**: `[Strapi] Reachability check failed — using DB-only until Strapi works: …` with the real error (`fetch failed`, TLS, 401, etc.).

4. **`server/storage.ts` (`HybridStorage.getAllBooks`)**  
   - If the **DB** list fails, it **logs a warning** and still **merges Strapi** when Strapi is reachable, so you are not blocked from Strapi-only books by a broken DB **for this route**.  
   - Other routes still need a working **`DATABASE_URL`**.

5. **`.env.example`**  
   - Short notes on **`#`** in passwords and **`%40`** for **`@`**.

---

### Why Strapi books did not show

1. **`getAllBooks` always hit Postgres first.** With a bad URL, that threw → **`/api/books` 500** before any Strapi merge. That is relaxed only for **`getAllBooks`** as above.  
2. **`[Pre-warm] Skipped: fetch failed`** means the server could not reach Strapi over the network (URL, DNS, TLS, firewall, token, etc.). After a restart, check the **new one-line** `[Strapi] Reachability check failed…` log for the exact reason.

---

### What you should do locally

1. Correct **`DATABASE_URL`** in **`.env`** (host **`localhost`**, proper password encoding / quoting).  
2. Restart **`npm run dev`**. If the URL is still wrong, startup should stop with **one** explicit error from **`resolveDatabaseUrl`**.  
3. For Strapi: confirm **`STRAPI_URL`** (no stray spaces; usually `https://your-cms-host` with **no** `/api` suffix — the code adds **`/api`**). Confirm **`STRAPI_API_TOKEN`** is valid for that instance.

---

Here is what that log is showing, in order, and what we changed.

### What each error was

1. **`listen ENOTSUP` with `reusePort`**  
   That comes from an **older** server build. Your current `server/index.ts` already uses `httpServer.listen(port, "0.0.0.0", …)` **without** `reusePort`. If you still see `ENOTSUP`, make sure you’ve saved the file and restarted dev.

2. **`DATABASE_URL, ensure the database is provisioned`**  
   That text was from an **older** `drizzle.config.ts` (before it used `resolveDatabaseUrl`). Current config loads `.env` and validates the URL.

3. **`getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND base` on `db:push` / `npm run dev`**  
   Usually either:
   - **`DATABASE_URL=DATABASE_URL=postgresql://...`** in `.env` (we fixed that once and added stripping), or  
   - A **bad `DATABASE_URL` exported in your shell** (e.g. in `~/.zshrc`). Node’s default `dotenv` behavior is **not** to override existing env vars, so the shell value kept winning and still parsed as host `base`.

4. **`EADDRINUSE` on port 5000**  
   Something else is already bound to **5000** (often another `npm run dev`). Use **`PORT=5050 npm run dev`** or stop the other process.

### Code updates (already applied)

- **`server/index.ts`**: Load env with **`dotenv.config({ path: ".env", override: process.env.NODE_ENV !== "production" })`** so **`.env` overrides** a bad exported `DATABASE_URL` in dev. Added a **`listen` error handler** that explains **`EADDRINUSE`** and exits cleanly.  
- **`drizzle.config.ts`**: Same **`override`** behavior before **`resolveDatabaseUrl()`**, so **`npm run db:push`** matches what the app uses.  
- **`server/database-url.ts`**: Strip a repeated **`DATABASE_URL=`** prefix in a **loop** so nested typos are cleaned.

### What you should run

```bash
npm run db:push
npm run dev
```

If 5000 is busy:

```bash
PORT=5050 npm run dev
```

Optional: clear a bad export for this session:

```bash
unset DATABASE_URL
npm run dev
```

Your **`.env`** line should look exactly like (one `=`, no duplicated key):

`DATABASE_URL=postgresql://postgres:…@localhost:5432/sacred_script_hub`

Here is what was going on and what we changed.

### Why `kill` did not help

On **macOS**, **AirPlay Receiver** often listens on **port 5000**. That is a **system** service, so it does not show up as your Node process and **`lsof | kill` on your app** does not free 5000.

Your **`.env` had `PORT=5000`**, so the app always tried 5000 and kept colliding.

### What we changed

1. **`server/index.ts`** — If **`PORT` is not set** and **`NODE_ENV === "development"`**, the server now defaults to **`5050`** instead of 5000. Production (e.g. `npm start` with `NODE_ENV=production`) still defaults to **5000** when `PORT` is unset. **`REPL_ID` is no longer used to pick the port** (a copied Replit `REPL_ID` was forcing 5000 locally).

2. **Your `.env`** — Removed **`PORT=5000`** and left a short comment so the new dev default applies.

3. **`.env.example`** — Restored to **safe placeholders** (it had been corrupted with duplicate `DATABASE_URL`, broken URLs, and partial secrets). **Rotate** any keys that ever sat in a committed `.env.example` if that file was pushed.

4. **Error copy** — `EADDRINUSE` now mentions **AirPlay** and trying another port.

### What you should do

Run:

```bash
npm run dev
```

Open **`http://localhost:5050`**.

If you **must** use 5000 locally: **System Settings → General → AirDrop & Handoff → AirPlay Receiver → Off**, then you can set **`PORT=5000`** in `.env` again.

The **`◇ injected env from .env`** lines are from **your tooling** (e.g. dotenvx / Cursor); they are not from this repo’s scripts.

**What was wrong:** Something else is already using **5050** (often another `npm run dev` or another app). Your shell only showed one failed bind, then exit.

**What we changed:** In **development**, if **`PORT` is not set** in `.env`, the server will **try 5050, then 5051, …** up to **40** ports until one binds. You’ll see short log lines like `port 5050 in use, trying 5051…`, then **`serving on port …`** on the first free port.

If **`PORT`** **is** set in `.env`, behavior is unchanged: it uses **only** that port (so production / Replit stay predictable).

Run **`npm run dev`** again and open the URL printed in the log (e.g. `http://localhost:5056`). To free old servers: **`lsof -iTCP:5050-5090 -sTCP:LISTEN`** then stop the PIDs you don’t need, or set **`PORT=5173`** (or any free port) in `.env` to pin one port.

Here is what that log is telling you, and what we changed in code.

### Why every line appears twice

That pattern almost always means **two Node processes** are running the app at the same time (e.g. two terminals both doing `npm run dev`, or Cursor running dev plus you running it again). Both hit the same DB and both run the seed/import pipeline, so logs are interleaved in pairs.

**What to do:** stop extras — `pkill -f "tsx server/index.ts"` (or quit other dev terminals) — then start **one** `npm run dev`.

A **per-process** guard was added so `runSeedOperations()` only runs once **in a single process** if something called it twice by mistake.

---

### `[Katha] JSON file not found`

The Katha seeder expects a Replit-era file under `attached_assets/`. In your repo, **`attached_assets/` only has an HTML file** — the JSON was never committed (often too large or Replit-only).

**What to do:** copy `Upanishads_Complete_Export_(1)_1771923200056.json` into `attached_assets/`, **or** any JSON whose name matches `*Upanishads*` / `*Katha*` / `*upanishad*` (the seeder now picks that up). Otherwise use **Strapi** for Katha content.

---

### `[Import] Book katha-upanishad-bhashya not found`

The import step looks for a book row with that slug. With Katha seed skipped, that book is missing, so the import correctly skips Katha.

---

### `[Pre-warm] Skipped: fetch failed`

Strapi prewarm could not complete a `fetch` (network, TLS, DNS, wrong URL, bad token, firewall, etc.). **`fetch failed`** is often a low-level network/TLS error; the catch block now logs **`cause`** when present so the next run should show a bit more detail.

Check **`STRAPI_URL`** / **`STRAPI_API_TOKEN`** and that this machine can reach the CMS (browser or `curl` the Strapi `/api/granthas` URL).

---

**Summary:** Stop duplicate dev servers; add the Katha JSON (or use Strapi); fix Strapi connectivity for pre-warm. The small code updates are in `server/index.ts` (seed guard + pre-warm error detail) and `server/seed-katha-upanishad.ts` (flexible JSON path + clearer error).

---

```bash
npm run dev
```

Here is what was going wrong and what we changed.

### What we verified

From your machine, `https://admincms.xoidlabs.com/api/granthas` behaves like this:

1. **Strict TLS** – `curl` failed with **“unable to get local issuer certificate”**, so Node’s `fetch` can fail with a generic **`fetch failed`** even when the URL and token are fine.
2. **With TLS verification turned off** – the request completes but the server answers **HTTP 403** with a **large HTML page** (not Strapi JSON). That usually means a **firewall / WAF / Zero Trust / IP allowlist** in front of the CMS, or the token is rejected before Strapi’s JSON API runs.

So the client was not “broken” in a small way; **the host is not returning the Strapi API to your laptop** (or not without VPN / office network / Cloudflare Access).

### What we changed in code (`server/strapi.ts`)

- Strapi calls now go through **`undici`** with an optional **`User-Agent`** (some gateways block anonymous clients).
- **`STRAPI_TLS_SKIP_VERIFY=1`** (**.env**, **local only**) uses an `undici` `Agent` with **`rejectUnauthorized: false`** for Strapi requests only, so **certificate chain** issues on dev machines can be worked around. **Do not use this in production.**
- On non-OK responses, the error includes a **short snippet of the response body** (so you can see “FortiGate”, “Cloudflare”, “Access denied”, etc.).
- On network/TLS failures, the error includes **`cause`** when present and points at **`STRAPI_TLS_SKIP_VERIFY`** for cert problems.
- **`testStrapiConnection()`** now uses the same path as **`strapiFetch`**, so **`GET /api/strapi/status`** matches real book fetching.

**Dependency:** `undici` is added as a direct dependency (used for the optional TLS agent).

### `.env.example`

Documents **`STRAPI_TLS_SKIP_VERIFY`**, **`STRAPI_TIMEOUT_MS`**, **`STRAPI_USER_AGENT`**.

### What you should do

1. **After pulling these changes**, open **`http://localhost:<port>/api/strapi/status`** (same host as the app). The `message` field should now spell out **403 + HTML snippet** or a **TLS** error.
2. If it’s **TLS**: add to **`.env`** (local only):  
   `STRAPI_TLS_SKIP_VERIFY=1`  
   Restart **`npm run dev`** and hit **`/api/strapi/status`** again.
3. If it’s still **403** with HTML: fix **infrastructure** – VPN / office network, **Cloudflare Access**, **IP allowlist**, or ask whoever runs **`admincms.xoidlabs.com`** to allow your IP or machine user-agent for **`/api/*`**. Regenerate a **Strapi API token** (Settings → API Tokens) with **read** on **`granthas`** if the token might be wrong or expired.

Until **`/api/strapi/status`** returns **`connected: true`**, **`HybridStorage`** will keep using **Postgres-only** books, so Strapi titles will not show in the list.
